source.title: AICPA 2017 Trust Services Criteria (revised Points of Focus, 2022)
source.wording: Omnisciente summaries; no licensed verbatim reproduction

CC1.1.review_note: Summary uses conduct-related Points of Focus to clarify ethical commitment; it does not prescribe a formal policy.

items.text: Management establishes expectations for ethical behavior and follows through when conduct falls short.
items.source_reference: CC1.1; conduct expectations and follow-through Points of Focus, page 15

items.text: Communicate conduct expectations during onboarding and when responsibilities change.
Provide a reporting route and assign responsibility for consistent follow-up.
Review recurring conduct concerns and whether corrective responses address their causes.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC1.1

items.text: Demonstrate a commitment to integrity.
Demonstrate a commitment to ethical values.

practical.summary: Demonstrate integrity and ethical conduct in practice.
review: Compare leadership's stated conduct expectations with how employees, contractors, and relevant provider personnel are expected to behave. Confirm people can recognize and report unacceptable conduct.
Examine how actual concerns were considered and addressed. A handbook alone does not resolve inconsistent treatment, ignored reports, or leadership behavior that contradicts stated expectations.
evidence: Leadership communications, handbook or conduct guidance, and onboarding records can show the expectations communicated; use the formats the organization actually relies on.
Redacted concern records, management decisions, or follow-up records can demonstrate the response to conduct issues without exposing unnecessary personal information.
outcome: Personnel understand the expected conduct, leadership acts consistently with it, and actual departures receive an appropriate response.
operational: Integrate conduct expectations and reporting routes into onboarding, provider engagement, and relevant role changes. Assign a responsible person to handle concerns consistently.
enhanced: Review patterns in conduct concerns and repeat issues to see whether the response changed behavior.

assessment_criteria.text: Demonstrate a commitment to integrity.
Demonstrate a commitment to ethical values.

CC1.2.review_note: Oversight arrangements depend on entity size and structure; see source footnote 15.

items.text: The governing body provides independent oversight of the development and performance of internal control.
Give the governing body control issues, decisions and unresolved actions in a usable briefing.
Have oversight members evaluate whether their challenge changed management decisions.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC1.2

items.text: Governance demonstrates independence from management, appropriate to the entity’s structure.
Governance oversees the development of internal control.
Governance oversees the performance of internal control.

practical.summary: Governance provides independent oversight of the control environment.
review: Identify who provides governance oversight, how management's decisions are challenged, and whether the oversight arrangement fits the organization's size and structure.

Trace significant risks, incidents, and control problems to oversight discussions and decisions across the review period. Attendance or receipt of a dashboard alone does not show that issues were considered.
evidence: Governance responsibilities and meeting or decision records can show who reviewed material issues, the questions raised, and the decisions made.
Briefing materials with dated follow-up can show whether oversight had the information and relevant expertise needed to act.
outcome: An appropriate governance body or arrangement meaningfully challenges management and follows the development and performance of controls.
operational: Prepare oversight updates around material changes, unresolved issues, and decisions needed. Set the review rhythm to the organization's risks and adopted governance commitments.
enhanced: Seek suitably independent expertise when governance lacks the knowledge to challenge a material technical or control issue.

assessment_criteria.text: Governance demonstrates independence from management, appropriate to the entity’s structure.
Governance oversees the development of internal control.
Governance oversees the performance of internal control.

CC1.3.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: Management establishes structures, reporting lines, authorities and responsibilities, with governing-body oversight, to support the organization's objectives.
Keep reporting lines and delegated decision rights accessible to control owners.
Clarify the handoffs between internal teams and outsourced providers.
Management establishes structures and reporting lines under governance oversight.
Management establishes appropriate authority and responsibilities to achieve objectives.

practical.summary: Assign structure, authority, and responsibilities that support objectives.
review: Trace important control decisions from the person doing the work to the person accountable for approval and escalation. Compare current responsibilities with the actual organization.

Confirm handoffs between the client, MSP/MSSP, and other providers identify who acts and who retains oversight. Look for unowned work, conflicting authority, and assignments left behind after role changes.
evidence: An organization chart, role descriptions, responsibility matrix, or service agreement can establish ownership. Approvals or escalation records can demonstrate that those arrangements are used.
outcome: People can identify who executes, approves, and escalates control work, including work shared with providers.
operational: Update responsibilities during staffing, service, and provider changes, and confirm the affected people understand the handoff.

assessment_criteria.text: Management establishes structures and reporting lines under governance oversight.
Management establishes appropriate authority and responsibilities to achieve objectives.

CC1.4.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization attracts, develops and retains people with the competence needed to achieve its objectives.
Connect hiring and development activities to the competencies of each control role.
Arrange cover for control responsibilities when key staff are absent.
Evaluate whether training resolves observed execution errors.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC1.4

items.text: Attract people with the competence needed for objectives.
Develop people’s competence to support objectives.
Retain competent people to support objectives.

practical.summary: Develop and retain people capable of meeting control responsibilities.
review: Compare the skills and capacity needed for security responsibilities with the people or providers assigned to them. Consider coverage when key personnel are unavailable.
Review hiring, role changes, and development activity during the period. Training completion alone may not address an unsupported technical responsibility or recurring execution errors.
evidence: Role requirements, relevant experience, training results, staffing reviews, or provider qualification records can explain why assigned personnel are capable of the work.
Dated development, hiring, or backup-coverage actions can show how identified competence and capacity gaps were addressed.
outcome: Assigned people have the capability and support to perform their responsibilities, and known skill or staffing gaps have an effective response.
operational: Include control responsibilities in role discussions and select development or provider support based on actual gaps, not only completion of general awareness training.
enhanced: Use a task walkthrough or practical exercise to validate capability for a critical responsibility where attendance records give limited assurance.

assessment_criteria.text: Attract people with the competence needed for objectives.
Develop people’s competence to support objectives.
Retain competent people to support objectives.

CC1.5.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization holds individuals accountable for their internal-control responsibilities.
Include control responsibilities in performance conversations and follow up on missed obligations.
Review whether delivery incentives encourage staff to bypass controls.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC1.5

items.text: Hold people accountable for their internal-control responsibilities in achieving objectives.

practical.summary: Hold people accountable for their control responsibilities.
review: Confirm owners understand the work and completion expectations assigned to them, including their responsibilities for outsourced activities.
Compare expected work with dated completion and management follow-up. Investigate repeated missed reviews, nominal owners who do not act, or performance pressures that encourage bypassing controls.
evidence: Responsibility assignments, completion records, owner reviews, or management decisions can show how performance was evaluated and missed responsibilities were addressed.
outcome: Accountability is visible in how work is performed and how management responds when assigned responsibilities are not met.
operational: Make expected completion, escalation, and backup ownership clear within existing work tracking and performance discussions.
enhanced: Compare recurring missed responsibilities across teams to identify workload or incentive problems that individual reminders do not resolve.

assessment_criteria.text: Hold people accountable for their internal-control responsibilities in achieving objectives.

CC2.1.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization obtains or generates and uses relevant, quality information for internal control.
Identify each control owner's information needs and the responsible data source.
Check important reports for missing, outdated or inconsistent information before use.
Reconcile a sample of management reports to their underlying records.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC2.1

items.text: Obtain or generate relevant information of suitable quality for internal control.
Use that information to support internal control.

practical.summary: Use reliable, relevant information to support controls.
review: Identify the reports, inventories, data flows, and other information that control owners actually use. Confirm their scope and source match the decision or review being performed.

Check report dates, filters, population coverage, and significant transformations. A current dashboard does not establish what information supported earlier reviews; missing systems or stale exports can undermine the result.
evidence: Exports with query parameters, source inventories, report definitions, or reconciliation records can demonstrate that review information is complete and reliable.
Dated review records tied to the information used can show which population and period were assessed.
outcome: Control decisions use information that is sufficiently accurate, complete, current, and traceable for their purpose.
operational: Assign ownership for important reporting sources and preserve the filters or scope needed to understand each review. Recheck reports after source or system changes.
enhanced: Reconcile a critical review population against an independent inventory or source to identify omissions that the report cannot reveal about itself.

assessment_criteria.text: Obtain or generate relevant information of suitable quality for internal control.
Use that information to support internal control.

CC2.2.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization communicates objectives and internal-control responsibilities to the people who need them.
Use role-specific communications for control changes and escalation routes.
Ask a sample of recipients to demonstrate how they would report a control concern.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC2.2

items.text: Communicate internal-control objectives internally.
Communicate internal-control responsibilities and other necessary information internally.

practical.summary: Communicate internally so people can carry out controls.
review: Confirm employees and contractors receive the objectives, responsibilities, system changes, and reporting instructions relevant to their work.

Review communications and relevant training across the period, including new hires and changed roles. Look for excluded groups, outdated instructions, or required acknowledgements that were never completed.
evidence: Onboarding or training records, policy distribution, change notices, team briefings, and acknowledgements where adopted can show what reached the relevant audience and when.
Internal reports and escalations can show that control owners and leadership received information needed to act.
outcome: People receive and understand the information needed to perform their roles and know how to raise a concern.
operational: Connect communications to onboarding, role changes, and material process changes. Choose channels and follow-up that fit the audience and the organization's communication controls.
enhanced: Ask personnel to explain a relevant reporting or security task to check whether the communication was understood, not merely delivered.

assessment_criteria.text: Communicate internal-control objectives internally.
Communicate internal-control responsibilities and other necessary information internally.

CC2.3.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization communicates with external parties about matters affecting internal control.
Assign owners for customer and supplier communications about responsibilities and changes.
Route incoming concerns to a responsible team and track the response.
Communicate with external parties about matters affecting internal control.

practical.summary: Exchange control-relevant information with external parties.
review: Identify which customers, providers, and other external parties need information about responsibilities, service commitments, system changes, or incidents, and how they can report concerns back.
Trace relevant events during the period to communication decisions and delivery. Check for stale contacts, unclear client/provider handoffs, or notifications that did not meet applicable commitments.
evidence: Service terms, responsibility agreements, support channels, or notification procedures can show the expected information exchange.
Dated messages, tickets, approvals, or communication logs can demonstrate that the appropriate parties received information and incoming concerns were handled.
outcome: External parties and the organization can exchange relevant information in time to perform their responsibilities and address control concerns.
operational: Maintain contact and approval routes for communication scenarios that matter to the service. Reconcile notification responsibilities with MSP/MSSP and other provider arrangements.

assessment_criteria.text: Communicate with external parties about matters affecting internal control.

CC3.1.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization states its objectives clearly enough to identify and assess risks to their achievement.
Connect scoped service commitments to clear objectives used in risk assessment.
Define objectives clearly enough to identify associated risks.
Define objectives clearly enough to assess associated risks.

practical.summary: Define objectives clearly enough to assess related risks.
review: Compare the service's security objectives with its actual customer commitments, system requirements, and operating context. Confirm the team can explain what it is trying to achieve.

Use the defined system boundary as context, then check whether the objectives are specific enough to identify a failure and assess its significance. A system inventory or a goal to pass an audit is not, by itself, a clear control objective.
evidence: Service commitments, internal objectives, relevant contract requirements, or management planning records can explain the outcomes the organization intends to achieve and the basis for assessing risk.
outcome: Control owners can connect the service's objectives to identifiable risks and explain what an unacceptable outcome would be.
operational: Keep objectives aligned when services, commitments, or scope change. Treat system-description preparation as readiness context rather than a substitute for clear objectives.

assessment_criteria.text: Define objectives clearly enough to identify associated risks.
Define objectives clearly enough to assess associated risks.

CC3.2.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization identifies and analyzes risks to its objectives and decides how those risks will be managed.
Record risk analysis, response decisions and accountable owners in the existing risk workflow.
Revisit risk decisions when threat or business assumptions change.
Challenge major risk assumptions using observed incidents and near misses.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC3.2

items.text: Identify risks to objectives across the organization.
Analyze identified risks to determine how they should be managed.

practical.summary: Identify and analyze risks that could prevent achieving objectives.
review: Trace important objectives to relevant threats, weaknesses, and business or provider dependencies. Confirm the risk assessment considers the actual environment rather than only a generic list.

Examine how likelihood, impact, existing controls, and remaining exposure inform treatment decisions. Missing dependencies, unexplained ratings, or acceptance without a reasoned assessment need follow-up.
evidence: A risk register, assessment notes, scenario analysis, or management risk decisions can show what was considered and why particular responses were selected.
System, incident, vulnerability, and vendor information can support the assumptions behind the assessment.
outcome: Material risks are understood well enough to make justified management decisions about how to address them.
operational: Use a consistent method, involve relevant service and technical owners, and revisit risk when the environment or important assumptions change.
enhanced: Challenge high-impact scenarios against incident experience and provider dependencies to identify optimistic assumptions or overlooked exposure.

assessment_criteria.text: Identify risks to objectives across the organization.
Analyze identified risks to determine how they should be managed.

CC3.3.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization considers the potential for fraud when assessing risks to its objectives.
Include realistic fraud scenarios and relevant participants in risk discussions.
Consider potential fraud when assessing risks to objectives.

practical.summary: Consider fraud when assessing risks to objectives.
review: Review credible ways personnel or outsiders could intentionally misuse access, conceal activity, manipulate control records, or take information or assets.

Check whether high-trust roles and workflows were considered realistically. A technical vulnerability list alone may miss deliberate bypass, collusion, or incentives to misrepresent control performance.
evidence: Fraud or misuse scenarios in risk discussions, investigation lessons, or privileged-workflow reviews can show the intentional abuse considered and the resulting risk decisions.
outcome: The risk assessment addresses plausible intentional abuse in the organization's systems and processes, not only accidental failure.
operational: Include process owners when considering misuse of privileged access or sensitive workflows, and revisit scenarios when access models or incentives change.

assessment_criteria.text: Consider potential fraud when assessing risks to objectives.

CC3.4.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization identifies and assesses changes that could significantly affect internal control.
Use business, technology and supplier change workflows to trigger risk reassessment.
Compare completed changes with risk reviews to identify missed triggers.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC3.4

items.text: Identify changes that could significantly affect internal control.
Assess how those significant changes affect internal control.

practical.summary: Assess changes that could materially affect controls.
review: Review significant changes in services, technology, leadership, vendors, and external risk conditions to determine which could affect the control environment.
Trace changes during the period to a risk decision and any needed control updates. Identify new dependencies, responsibilities, or threats that left the assessment and controls out of date.
evidence: Business or technology change records, revised risk assessments, provider-change reviews, or management decisions can connect a significant change to its control impact and response.
outcome: Material changes are recognized and evaluated early enough for controls and responsibilities to remain appropriate.
operational: Add risk-impact prompts to existing service, vendor, organizational, and technology change workflows instead of relying only on a calendar review.
enhanced: Compare major changes recorded by business and technical teams against the risk-review record to find changes that bypassed assessment.

assessment_criteria.text: Identify changes that could significantly affect internal control.
Assess how those significant changes affect internal control.

CC4.1.review_note: Ongoing or separate evaluation is already part of the criterion, not an optional assurance upgrade.

items.text: The organization performs appropriate ongoing or separate evaluations to determine whether internal control is present and functioning.
Assign evaluation scope, responsibilities and timing based on control risk.
Compare conclusions from different evaluators where results conflict.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC4.1

items.text: Select and develop ongoing or separate evaluations of internal control.
Perform evaluations to determine whether internal-control components exist and function.

practical.summary: Evaluate whether controls are present and working.
review: Identify how management checks that controls work, including relevant provider-operated activities. Confirm evaluations cover the controls and risks the organization actually relies on.

Examine evaluation results, missed checks, and repeat exceptions across the review period. A completed-task count or a current configuration screenshot does not establish consistent control operation.
evidence: Dated control reviews, monitoring results, internal assessments, or relevant external assessments can show what was evaluated, the period covered, and what the reviewer found.
Provider results considered alongside client-side responsibilities can support monitoring of shared controls; the provider's involvement alone is insufficient.
outcome: Evaluations give management a supported view of whether its controls are functioning and reveal missed or ineffective activity.
operational: Define review scope and frequency according to risk, change, and adopted commitments. Include outcomes and exceptions, not just evidence collection or task completion.
enhanced: Use a reviewer separate from the operator for a higher-risk control to challenge the conclusion using the underlying records.

assessment_criteria.text: Select and develop ongoing or separate evaluations of internal control.
Perform evaluations to determine whether internal-control components exist and function.

CC4.2.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: Control deficiencies are evaluated and communicated promptly to those responsible for correction, including appropriate leadership.
Assign remediation owners and track deficiencies through the existing Findings and Actions workflows.
Have someone other than the action owner challenge closure support for significant deficiencies.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC4.2

items.text: Evaluate internal-control deficiencies promptly.
Communicate deficiencies promptly to those responsible for correction, including management and governance where appropriate.

practical.summary: Evaluate control deficiencies and communicate them for corrective action.
review: Trace identified control problems to an assessment of impact and communication to people able to correct them, with leadership involvement appropriate to significance.
Examine overdue, recurring, and closed items. Confirm closure reflects the actual result, not just a ticket status, and keep an unmet outcome visible when management accepts the associated risk.
evidence: Issue records, escalation messages, management decisions, and dated correction or retest records can show who was informed, what happened, and whether the deficiency remains.
outcome: Responsible people receive actionable information promptly, management can see unresolved exposure, and claimed corrections have support.
operational: Use the existing issue workflow to assign responsibility, set appropriate follow-up expectations, and record closure criteria. Opening an Action or approving an exception does not establish that the affected criterion is met.
enhanced: Review recurring deficiencies across teams to distinguish isolated mistakes from a control design or resourcing problem.

assessment_criteria.text: Evaluate internal-control deficiencies promptly.
Communicate deficiencies promptly to those responsible for correction, including management and governance where appropriate.

CC5.1.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization selects and develops control activities that reduce risks to acceptable levels.
Map selected controls to the risks they address and explain any compensating arrangements.
Select control activities that reduce risks to objectives to acceptable levels.
Develop the selected risk-reducing control activities.

practical.summary: Select controls that reduce risks to acceptable levels.
review: Connect the organization's significant risks to the controls selected to address them. Confirm each control has a plausible purpose in the actual service and operating model.

Walk through how the selected controls prevent or detect the relevant failure. Look for uncovered risks, incompatible responsibilities, or controls whose stated purpose is unsupported by how they work.
evidence: Risk-to-control mappings, process walkthroughs, control design notes, or management decisions can explain why controls were selected and how they reduce the identified exposure.
outcome: The selected control activities address the organization's risks with a justified basis for the remaining exposure.
operational: Record enough about each selected control to make its purpose, operator, trigger, and expected result understandable. Reconsider the design when risks or responsibilities change.

assessment_criteria.text: Select control activities that reduce risks to objectives to acceptable levels.
Develop the selected risk-reducing control activities.

CC5.2.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization establishes general control activities over technology that support its objectives.
Identify technology dependencies and assign ownership of supporting access, change and maintenance controls.
Select general technology control activities that support objectives.
Develop the selected general technology control activities.

practical.summary: Technology controls support the organization's objectives.
review: Identify technology and automated processes relied on by important controls, then examine the supporting access, infrastructure, and change arrangements.

Confirm client and provider responsibilities cover the relevant technology. Use dated records to distinguish a configured control from one that remained managed during the period; investigate unmanaged services or unsupported assumptions about provider coverage.
evidence: Architecture and responsibility records, configuration exports, access reviews, or change and maintenance records can connect technology dependencies to the controls protecting them.
outcome: Technology-dependent controls have supporting safeguards appropriate to the systems and risks on which they rely.
operational: Include supporting technology controls when a service is introduced or changed. Make client-side duties explicit where an MSP, cloud service, or other provider performs part of the work.

assessment_criteria.text: Select general technology control activities that support objectives.
Develop the selected general technology control activities.

CC5.3.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: Policies establish expectations for control activities.
Procedures put those control expectations into action.
Make procedures accessible to the people performing them and establish how exceptions are handled.
Compare actual execution with the procedure after significant operational changes.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC5.3

items.text: Establish policy expectations for control activities.
Deploy procedures that put those policies into operation.

practical.summary: Turn policy expectations into operating control procedures.
review: Compare stated policies and control expectations with the steps, ownership, and timing used in day-to-day work. No particular policy title or separate document for every topic is assumed.

Trace selected procedures to dated execution records throughout the review period. Look for procedures that no longer match systems, missed organization-defined frequencies, or approved policies with no evidence of use.
evidence: Policies, runbooks, workflow instructions, or embedded approval rules can explain how expectations are put into practice.
Tickets, review records, approvals, or other dated results can show that the procedure was followed and identified problems were acted on.
outcome: Operational work follows the organization's stated control expectations, and procedures remain usable and aligned with actual practice.
operational: Maintain procedures where operators use them, with clear owners and organization-defined triggers or frequencies. Update affected instructions when the service or control changes.
enhanced: Observe or reperform a higher-risk workflow to identify differences between the written procedure and routine execution.

assessment_criteria.text: Establish policy expectations for control activities.
Deploy procedures that put those policies into operation.

CC6.1.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization implements logical-access security over protected information assets to protect them from security events.
Identify protected assets and access paths, then apply authentication and access rules appropriate to their risks.
Include access-control decisions in architecture reviews.
Validate that a sample of disallowed access attempts is blocked across different access paths.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC6.1

items.text: Implement logical-access security across software, infrastructure, and architecture to protect information assets against security events.

practical.summary: Protect information assets through logical access safeguards.
review: Compare the in-scope systems, data stores, integrations, and access paths with the safeguards actually applied. Look for unmanaged systems or access routes outside the expected controls.

Confirm authentication, access restrictions, and credential protection match the organization's risks and commitments, including service accounts, privileged access, and provider-managed access. Examine MFA or encryption wherever the organization relies on them.
evidence: Architecture or inventory records alongside identity, application, or network configuration exports can demonstrate coverage and the protections in use.
Dated configuration changes, authentication records, or review results can show whether safeguards continued to operate during the period; a current settings screenshot shows only the current state.
outcome: Access safeguards cover the protected environment and match the organization's selected controls; unmanaged access paths or ineffective protections remain identifiable gaps.
operational: Maintain a usable link between systems, owners, access methods, and control settings. Assign responsibility for service credentials and key handling, including handoffs to the MSP or other providers.
enhanced: Validate selected access paths from an unauthorized-user perspective to check whether the configured restrictions work as intended.

assessment_criteria.text: Implement logical-access security across software, infrastructure, and architecture to protect information assets against security events.

CC6.2.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: For access administered by the organization, internal and external users are registered and authorized before credentials or access are issued.
For access administered by the organization, credentials are removed when user access is no longer authorized.
Connect credential approval and removal to joiner, mover and leaver workflows.
Review credentials for accounts without a current owner or business purpose.
Reconcile account records with personnel and supplier records to identify missed removals.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC6.2

items.text: Register new internal and external users before issuing credentials or granting organization-administered access.
Authorize those users before issuing credentials or granting access.
Remove organization-administered credentials when access is no longer authorized.

practical.summary: Authorize credentials before granting access; revoke obsolete credentials.
review: Trace new employee, contractor, vendor, and non-person accounts to the authorization that preceded access being granted.

Compare departures and access-ending events with actual disablement or credential removal across the systems administered by the organization. Look for stale accounts, missed applications, and incomplete provider handoffs.
evidence: Access requests and approvals paired with provisioning logs can demonstrate who authorized access and when it became effective.
Dated termination records, account exports, and disablement tickets across the review period can demonstrate removal, including failures discovered after the initial offboarding task.
outcome: Accounts are authorized before use and credentials cease to work when authorization ends; closing an offboarding ticket alone is not evidence of removal.
operational: Use a joiner/leaver workflow that names each system owner and distinguishes work completed by the client from work awaiting its provider. Review account validity at the organization's defined frequency.
enhanced: Reconcile active accounts to personnel and third-party rosters to find accounts missed by event-driven provisioning and removal workflows.

assessment_criteria.text: Register new internal and external users before issuing credentials or granting organization-administered access.
Authorize those users before issuing credentials or granting access.
Remove organization-administered credentials when access is no longer authorized.

CC6.3.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization grants, changes and removes access according to roles, responsibilities and system design, considering least privilege and segregation of duties.
Document role entitlements and approval responsibilities for access changes.
Review privileges and incompatible access when responsibilities change.
Test effective permissions rather than relying only on the requested access list.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC6.3

items.text: Authorize access according to roles, responsibilities, and system design.
Modify or remove access when roles, responsibilities, or systems change.
Consider least privilege when managing access.
Consider segregation of duties when managing access.

practical.summary: Keep permissions aligned with roles and appropriate separation.
review: Compare effective permissions, privileged roles, and shared or service-account access with approved job or system needs, including conflicting responsibilities.
Trace role changes and access reviews to actual permission changes or removals. Identify excessive privileges and reviews that signed off access without resolving the identified mismatch.
evidence: Role/group exports, permission rules, and approvals can show how access reflects responsibilities and separates incompatible activities.
Dated role-change tickets or access-review decisions paired with implementation records can show that decisions took effect during the period.
outcome: Permissions remain appropriate as responsibilities change, and incompatible access is restricted or addressed through the organization's selected controls.
operational: Assign owners to privileged and non-person accounts. Give access reviewers enough business context to challenge access, with review timing based on the organization's risks and adopted controls.
enhanced: Compare actual privilege use with approved need to identify long-unused administration rights or combinations missed by role-based reviews.

assessment_criteria.text: Authorize access according to roles, responsibilities, and system design.
Modify or remove access when roles, responsibilities, or systems change.
Consider least privilege when managing access.
Consider segregation of duties when managing access.

CC6.4.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: The organization restricts physical access to relevant facilities and protected information assets to authorized personnel.
Assign responsibility for visitor access, badge changes and recovery of physical devices.
Restrict physical access to facilities to authorized people.
Restrict physical access to protected information assets to authorized people.

practical.summary: Limit physical access to authorized people.
review: Identify relevant facilities, equipment, and media locations, including outsourced hosting, and confirm how physical access is restricted at each.
Review access grants, visitor arrangements, and removals against actual personnel needs. Check for active badges after departure or unclear responsibilities between the client and facility provider.
evidence: Badge/key records, visitor logs, access approvals, or dated removal records can demonstrate how restrictions operate; relevant provider assurance can support outsourced locations when its scope and customer responsibilities are evaluated.
outcome: Relevant physical assets and locations have working access restrictions, with client and provider responsibilities understood; cloud hosting alone does not establish that no physical controls apply.
operational: Include badges, keys, and equipment custody in personnel changes. Review physical access at a frequency suited to the organization's selected controls and locations.

assessment_criteria.text: Restrict physical access to facilities to authorized people.
Restrict physical access to protected information assets to authorized people.

CC6.5.review_note: No source gap identified for this criterion summary; control design remains entity-specific.

items.text: Protection of physical assets continues until recoverability of their data and software has been reduced and is no longer needed for organizational objectives.
Keep asset protection in place until the disposal or transfer owner confirms the selected sanitization outcome.
Validate sanitization results for a sample of retired assets, including supplier-handled disposal.
items.source_reference: Omnisciente additional assurance guidance for CC6.5

items.text: Reduce the ability to read or recover data and software before ending logical or physical protection of physical assets.
End protection only when recovering that data and software is no longer needed for objectives.

practical.summary: Sanitize retired assets before releasing their protections.
review: Examine how devices and media are retired, reused, returned, or transferred, and when their access protections or custody end.

Confirm data and software no longer needed on those assets are made inaccessible before protection ends. Look for assets released before wiping, unverifiable destruction, or unresolved provider disposal responsibilities.
evidence: Asset retirement records linked to wipe results, destruction records, return tickets, or provider confirmation can demonstrate the method, affected asset, timing, and completion.
outcome: Retired or released physical assets no longer expose recoverable information that needed protection; a disposal request without completed sanitization is insufficient.
operational: Keep assets under controlled custody until the selected sanitization method is confirmed. Include leased devices, removable media, and disposal vendors in the retirement workflow.

context.categories: These are assessment guidance categories, not AICPA maturity levels or mandatory stages.
context.obligations: Assess the organization's selected controls and commitments. A practice is not optional merely because it appears under Operational Practices or Enhanced Assurance. Set review frequencies to the organization's risks and obligations, not a universal SOC 2 cadence.
context.evidence: Use relevant examples or equivalent support from the client, MSP/MSSP or responsible provider; not every artifact is needed. Confirm what each party performs and what the records demonstrate.
context.type2: For Type 2 readiness, distinguish a documented design from consistent operation across the review period. Examine dated records, completion history, exceptions and follow-up. A current policy or screenshot alone does not establish historical operating effectiveness.
context.gaps: Opening an Action, recording an exception or accepting risk does not establish that an unmet criterion is satisfied.
context.baseline: Before assessing criteria, establish the service boundary, commitments, systems, data flows, providers and shared responsibilities. Maintain the system description as program context; it is not an extra TSC control checklist. Security-only scope still includes relevant incident recovery and business-disruption mitigations.
